entry: Method of representing three-dimensional objects on a flat surface so that they appear to recede in depth. In linear perspective, objects appear smaller as their distance from the observer increases, and receding lines converge toward vanishing points, usually on the horizon line. Systematic attempts date to around the fifth century BC in ancient Greece, where [[Aristotle]]'s *Poetics* described *skenographia*, the use of flat stage panels to give an illusion of depth. The philosophers Anaxagoras and [[Democritus]] developed geometric theories of perspective for it, and [[Euclid]] argued in his *Optics* (c. 300 BC) that perceived size is not a simple proportion of distance. Italian Renaissance artists, including [[Filippo Brunelleschi]], [[Leon Battista Alberti]], [[Masaccio]] and [[Leonardo da Vinci]], studied linear perspective, wrote treatises on it and incorporated it into their work. Chinese artists used oblique projection from the first or second century until the 18th century.

Capital and largest city of [[Western Australia]] (pop., 2023: over 2.2 million). Perth lies mostly on the Swan Coastal Plain between the Indian Ocean and the Darling Scarp, and is the fourth most populous city in [[Australia]]. The area is traditional land of the Whadjuk Noongar people, where [[Aboriginal Australians]] have lived for at least 48,000 years. Founded in 1829 by Captain James Stirling as the administrative center of the Swan River Colony, Perth was named after Perth, Scotland, and proclaimed a city by [[Queen Victoria]] in 1856. The colony accepted transported convicts from 1850 to supply labor for public works and construction. Mining booms in the late 20th and early 21st centuries made Perth the regional headquarters for major mining operations. Kings Park and Botanic Garden, one of the world's largest inner-city parks, is the most visited of the city's parks. All five of Western Australia's universities are based in Perth.

Country in western [[South America]], with Pacific coastal plains, the Andes and Amazon rainforest. At 1,285,216 sq km (496,225 sq mi), it is the third largest country in South America. Its capital and largest city is [[Lima]]. Its heritage traces back to the 10th millennium BCE and the [[Caral–Supe civilization]], the earliest in the Americas. The [[Inca Empire]] was the largest known state in the pre-Columbian Americas. The [[Spanish Empire]] conquered the region in the 16th century, and Peru formally proclaimed independence from Spain in 1821, completing it in 1824. Exploitation of guano brought a period of relative stability that ended with the [[War of the Pacific]] (1879–84). Peru is a representative democratic republic divided into 25 regions, with mining, manufacturing, agriculture and fishing as its main economic activities. Spanish is the main language, though many Peruvians speak [[Quechuan languages]].

Dietary practice in which [[Seafood|seafood]] is the only source of meat, often combined with eggs and dairy. The term, a portmanteau of the Italian *pesce* (fish) and [[Vegetarianism|vegetarian]], was coined in the United Kingdom in the late 1980s. Research from 2017 to 2018 estimated that approximately 3% of adults worldwide are pescetarian. Some biographers suspect [[Pythagoras]] ate fish, which would make him a pescetarian by modern standards. In [[Manichaeism]], the Hearers ate fish, grain and vegetables, but land animals were forbidden.

Capital and largest city of [[Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]] province, northwestern Pakistan. Located in the Peshawar Valley east of the Khyber Pass, it is the eighth most populous Pakistani city, with over 1.9 million residents. Its recorded history dates back to at least the sixth century BC, and as *Puruṣapura* it was the capital of the [[Kushan Empire]] under Kanishka in the second century CE. Muslim empires ruled after the Ghaznavid conquest of 1001 CE. It was an important trading center of the [[Mughal Empire]] and the winter capital of the Durrani Empire from 1776 until the Sikh Empire took it in 1823. The [[East India Company]] annexed it in 1849, and it became part of the [[British Raj]]. It became capital of the North-West Frontier Province in 1901 and part of Pakistan after the [[Partition of India]] in 1947. After Afghan refugees arrived following the [[Soviet–Afghan War]], the city shifted from a Hindko- to a Pashto-speaking city, and it is now largely populated by [[Pashtuns]].

Substance or biological agent that controls pests, including insects, plant pathogens, [[Weed|weeds]], nematodes and birds. Herbicides are the most common type, accounting for approximately 50% of global pesticide use. Until the 1950s, pesticides were mainly [[Inorganic compound|inorganic compounds]] and plant extracts. Persistent compounds such as [[DDT]] were banned many years ago, except for spraying houses against [[Malaria]] vectors. Global agricultural pesticide use reached 3.73 million tonnes of active ingredients in 2023, concentrated in [[China]], the [[United States]] and Brazil. Pesticides increase crop yields, but they carry drawbacks, including potential toxicity to humans and other species, pest resistance and bioaccumulation in ecosystems.

Animal kept primarily for companionship rather than as a working animal, [[Livestock|livestock]] or laboratory animal. [[Dog|Dogs]] and [[Cat|cats]] are the most popular pets, and others include rabbits, [[Ferret|ferrets]], [[Hamster|hamsters]], [[Parrot|parrots]], [[Frog|frogs]], fish and tarantulas. Pets can provide physical and emotional benefits: walking a dog gives both owner and dog exercise and social interaction, and therapy animals visit people in hospitals and nursing homes. People most often keep pets for companionship, to protect a home, or for the beauty of the animals. Keeping pets can harm their health if their needs are not met. Chocolate or grapes can be fatal to dogs, and philodendrons and Easter lilies can cause severe kidney damage in cats. In the United States there are approximately 86.4 million pet cats and 78.2 million pet dogs.

English synth-pop duo formed in [[London]] in 1981, consisting of Chris Lowe and Neil Tennant. The duo has sold more than 100 million records and had four UK number-one singles, including "West End Girls", "It's a Sin" and "Heart". Their sound centers on synth-pop and dance-pop, influenced early on by [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] and Hi-NRG, and later by house, eurodance and EDM. They have been nominated for four [[Grammy Awards]] and have won three Brit Awards. Their album *Release* (2002) blended orchestral and acoustic elements with synthesizers.

American [[Basketball|basketball]] player nicknamed Pistol Pete. He is the all-time top scorer in NCAA Division I men's basketball, with 3,667 points at an average of 44.2 per game for Louisiana State University. Selected by the Atlanta Hawks in the 1970 NBA draft, he also played for the New Orleans Jazz and finished with the [[Boston Celtics]]. He was named an All-Star five times and All-NBA four times. He was considered among the best ball handlers ever to play. He died suddenly at age 40 during a pickup game, because of an undetected heart defect.

American [[Baseball|baseball]] player and manager, nicknamed Charlie Hustle. He played in [[Major League Baseball]] from 1963 to 1986, mainly for the [[Cincinnati]] Reds, and won three [[World Series]] championships. He holds the MLB record for career hits (4,256). In August 1989 he was permanently barred from baseball amid accusations that he had gambled on games, including games involving his own team. He admitted in 2004 that he had bet on baseball but said he never bet on his team to lose. He was posthumously reinstated in 2025 and became eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.

English musician and songwriter, co-founder, guitarist and principal songwriter of [[The Who|the Who]]. He wrote more than 100 songs for 12 of the band's studio albums, including the rock operas *Tommy* (1969) and *Quadrophenia* (1973). He also plays keyboards, banjo, [[Accordion|accordion]], harmonica and mandolin, all self-taught. He received the Brit Award for Lifetime Achievement in 1983 and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1990 as a member of the Who. Ranked No. 3 in Dave Marsh's 1994 list of best guitarists, he has also written newspaper articles, books and scripts.

French philosopher, logician and theologian, regarded as one of the most brilliant and controversial theologians of his time. Born at Pallet, near [[Nantes]], he became a popular lecturer in [[Paris]]. His academic career was cut short after his love affair with his student and eventual wife, Héloïse d'Argenteuil, which later became the best-known aspect of his life. In philosophy he challenged the prevailing orthodoxy, and his logical treatment of the problem of universals, through nominalism and conceptualism, is celebrated. He pioneered the role of intent in [[Ethics|ethics]]. In Catholic [[Theology|theology]] he was condemned for his teaching on the [[Trinity]]. He is known for developing the concept of limbo and for the moral influence theory of atonement. His letters, including *The History of My Calamities*, helped set the tone for later epistolary novels.

Dutch-American physicist and physical chemist, and Nobel laureate in [[Chemistry]]. Born in Maastricht, he studied electrical engineering at Aachen and in 1906 followed Arnold Sommerfeld to Munich as his assistant. In 1912 he extended [[Albert Einstein]]'s theory of specific heat to lower temperatures, and he applied the concept of dipole moment to asymmetric molecules; the units of molecular dipole moments are termed debyes in his honor. In 1923, with Erich Hückel, he improved [[Svante Arrhenius]]'s theory of electrical conductivity in electrolyte solutions. He later directed the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics in Berlin, succeeding Einstein. In 1940 he moved to the United States to chair the chemistry department at [[Cornell University]]. His service in German scientific bodies under the Nazi regime remains controversial: critics allege he helped dismiss Jewish colleagues, while supporters argue he sought to preserve institutions and aid persecuted scientists.

American actor known for playing Tyrion Lannister in the HBO series [[Game of Thrones]], for which he won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series a record four times. Born in the North Jersey region of [[New Jersey]], he studied acting at Bennington College. His breakthrough came with the comedy-drama *The Station Agent* (2003). His other films include *Elf* (2003), *X-Men: Days of Future Past* (2014) and *Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri* (2017). He also performed on stage, including the title role in *Richard III* at the Public Theatre.

American actor best known for playing the rumpled detective [[Columbo|Lieutenant Columbo]] in the NBC series *Columbo*, which earned him four Primetime Emmy Awards. He lost his right eye to retinoblastoma at age three and wore an artificial eye, which caused his trademark squint. He was twice nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor, and he was the first actor nominated for an Academy Award and an Emmy in the same year, achieving this twice. He often worked with [[John Cassavetes]]. He received a posthumous star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2013.

English singer-songwriter, musician and human rights activist. He co-founded [[Genesis (band)|Genesis]] and was its lead vocalist until 1975, then had a successful solo career. His album *So* (1986) became his best-selling release, and its single "Sledgehammer" won a record nine awards at the 1987 [[MTV]] Video Music Awards. He co-founded the World of Music, Arts and Dance (WOMAD) festival in 1982 and wrote the soundtrack for [[Martin Scorsese]]'s *The Last Temptation of Christ* (1988). His protest song "Biko" addressed [[Apartheid]] in South Africa. In 2007 he developed the idea for The Elders with [[Nelson Mandela]] and [[Richard Branson]].

German mathematician, known for work in number theory, analysis and mathematical physics. In number theory he proved special cases of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] and created [[Analytic number theory|analytic number theory]]. In analysis he advanced the theory of [[Fourier series]] and was one of the first to give the modern formal definition of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]]. In mathematical physics he studied potential theory, boundary-value problems, heat diffusion and hydrodynamics. Born in Düren, then part of the French Empire, he studied at a Jesuit gymnasium in [[Cologne]], where [[Georg Ohm]] helped widen his mathematical knowledge. He taught in Berlin from 1828 and in 1855 succeeded [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] at the [[University of Göttingen]].

New Zealand filmmaker, best known as director, screenwriter and producer of the [[The Lord of the Rings (film series)|Lord of the Rings]] trilogy and [[The Hobbit|Hobbit]] trilogy, both adapted from novels by [[J. R. R. Tolkien]]. *The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King* (2003) won three [[Academy Awards]], including Best Picture. He also directed *Braindead* (1992), *Heavenly Creatures* (1994), *King Kong* (2005) and the World War I documentary *They Shall Not Grow Old* (2018). Knighted in 2010, he received an honorary Palme d'Or at the 79th [[Cannes Film Festival]] in May 2026.

Russian [[Anarchism|anarchist]] political philosopher and geographer, a proponent of anarchist [[Communism|communism]]. Born into an aristocratic land-owning family, he served as an officer in [[Siberia]], where he took part in geological expeditions. He was imprisoned for his activism in 1874 and escaped two years later, then spent 41 years in exile in Switzerland, France and England. He envisioned a decentralized communist society of self-governing communities and worker-run enterprises, free from central [[State (polity)|state]] government. His works include *The Conquest of Bread* (1892) and *Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution* (1902). He returned to Russia after the [[Russian Revolution]] in 1917 but was disappointed by the Bolshevik state.

English and Irish actor, known for work on stage and screen. Born in [[Leeds]], he trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art and became a Shakespearean actor at the Bristol Old Vic. In 1963 he played the title role in *Hamlet* in the National Theatre's first production. He received his first Academy Award nomination for Best Actor for portraying [[T. E. Lawrence]] in *Lawrence of Arabia* (1962). He was further nominated for playing King Henry II in *Becket* (1964) and *The Lion in Winter* (1968). He holds the record for the most Oscar nominations for acting without a win, tied with [[Glenn Close]]. He received an honorary Academy Award in 2002, and he voiced the restaurant critic Anton Ego in the [[Pixar]] film *Ratatouille* (2007).

Fictional boy who can fly and never grows up, created by Scottish novelist and playwright J. M. Barrie. Peter leads the Lost Boys on the island of Neverland, where he has adventures with fairies, pirates, [[Mermaid|mermaids]] and Native Americans. He first appeared in Barrie's novel *The Little White Bird* (1902). Barrie then put him at the center of the [[Play (theatre)|play]] *Peter Pan; or, The Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up*, which premiered in 1904 at the Duke of York's Theatre in [[London]]. Barrie later adapted the play as the novel *Peter and Wendy* (1911). In the book and play, Peter carries a [[Dagger|dagger]] for cutting and a [[Sword|sword]] for fighting. Barrie gave the copyright to Great Ormond Street Children's Hospital in 1929, and the hospital still collects royalties from UK adaptations.

Flemish artist and diplomat, considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque tradition. His compositions reference classical and Christian history, and his style emphasized movement, color and sensuality, following the dramatic art promoted in the [[Counter-Reformation]]. He ran a large workshop in [[Antwerp]] that produced paintings for nobility and collectors throughout Europe, including altarpieces, portraits, landscapes and history paintings. His catalog of works lists 1,403 pieces, excluding copies made in his workshop. He also designed tapestries and prints, and wrote a book on the palaces of [[Genoa]], published in 1622. Knighted by both Philip IV of Spain and [[Charles I of England]], he was also an avid art collector and sold art to George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham.

Danish former professional footballer and goalkeeper. During eight seasons at Manchester United he won 15 trophies, including five Premier League titles, and captained the club to victory in the 1999 [[UEFA Champions League]]. He won the [[UEFA European Championship]] with Denmark in 1992 and played 129 games for his country between 1987 and 2001. He was voted IFFHS World's Best Goalkeeper in 1992 and 1993. In a 2001 [[Reuters]] poll, most of the 200,000 participants voted him the best goalkeeper in history. Born in Gladsaxe, [[Copenhagen]], he also played for Brøndby, Sporting CP and Aston Villa.

English actor and comedian, known for his versatility and for playing Chief Inspector Clouseau in *The Pink Panther* series. He first gained fame on [[BBC]] Radio in *The Goon Show* (1951–60).His films include *Lolita* (1962), in which he played the sinister Clare Quilty, and *Dr. Strangelove* (1964), directed by [[Stanley Kubrick]], in which he played three roles. He won a BAFTA Award for *I'm All Right Jack* (1959) and was twice nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor. Many of his films feature [[Satire|satire]] and black humor. He struggled with depression and frequently clashed with directors and co-stars.

English [[Serial killer|serial killer]] known as the Yorkshire Ripper. He was convicted of murdering thirteen women and girls and attempting to murder seven others between 1975 and 1980. Most of the murders took place in [[West Yorkshire]], and two in [[Manchester]]. He was arrested in [[Sheffield]] in January 1981 for driving with false number plates. He confessed, saying the voice of God had sent him to kill prostitutes. He was convicted by majority verdict. He was diagnosed with paranoid [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]] and received a whole life order. He died from complications of [[Diabetes|diabetes]].
